33.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the exaltation of Jesus is the key to receiving the Holy Spirit, demonstrating that Christ's authority is essential for God's work in the world. The outpouring of the Holy Spirit marks the beginning of a new era for believers, where they are equipped to live and testify to their faith.
33.commentaire: The exaltation of Jesus at the right hand of God reminds us that our faith rests on a living and exalted Savior. By receiving the Holy Spirit, we are called to live in God's power, transforming our lives and those around us. This verse encourages us to recognize the work of the Holy Spirit in our lives and to be faithful witnesses of the Gospel.

mots.sens: This word means 'Lord' and is used in the New Testament to refer to both God and Jesus Christ. In this verse, it emphasizes the divine authority and sovereignty of the risen Christ. The distinction between 'my Lord' and 'The Lord' highlights the unique relationship between God the Father and Jesus, thus revealing the trinitarian nature of God.

This term means 'to sit' and evokes the idea of taking a position of authority or reign. In the context of this verse, it indicates that Jesus, after His resurrection, was exalted and took His place at the right hand of God, a position of power and honor. This underscores the fulfillment of prophecies concerning the Messiah and His role in the plan of salvation.

34.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the 1st century, shortly after the resurrection of Jesus, at a time when the early Christians were seeking to understand and proclaim the divine nature of Christ in the face of a complex Jewish and Roman culture.
34.passage: Acts 2 recounts the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit descends upon the apostles. Peter, in his speech, quotes this verse to affirm the resurrection of Jesus and His exalted position, thus establishing a foundation for the Christian faith.
34.culture: In Jewish culture, the idea of a Messiah sitting at the right hand of God was deeply rooted in the scriptures, symbolizing divine authority. This would have resonated powerfully with Peter's Jewish listeners, reinforcing their understanding of Jesus as the promised Messiah.
34.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the reality of Jesus' resurrection and His ascension to heaven, affirming His divinity and central role in God's plan. It reminds believers that Jesus is alive and reigns, and that He is our intercessor before the Father.
34.commentaire: This passage calls us to recognize Christ's authority in our lives. Understanding that Jesus is seated at the right hand of God encourages us to live in confidence and assurance, knowing that our Savior has triumphed over death and reigns over all things. It compels us to boldly proclaim the Gospel, testifying to the power of His resurrection.

mots.sens: This term literally means 'footstool' or 'supporting foot.' It evokes the idea of a support or base upon which something rests. In the context of this verse, it symbolizes the domination and subjugation of Christ's enemies, who will ultimately be placed under His feet. This underscores God's sovereignty and Christ's ultimate victory over His adversaries.

This word designates an 'enemy' or 'adversary.' It comes from a root that implies opposition and hostility. In the context of this verse, it refers to those who oppose God's will and His kingdom. This highlights the spiritual struggle between good and evil, and the certainty that, despite this opposition, God has the final control.

35.epoque: This verse is set in the context of the 1st century, at a time when the early Christians faced opposition and persecution. This historical moment is marked by the proclamation of Jesus' resurrection and the establishment of the early Church.
35.passage: Acts 2 describes Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit descends upon the apostles, enabling them to preach with power. Verse 35 is part of a quotation from Psalm 110, highlighting the majesty and authority of Christ in the fulfillment of prophecy.
35.culture: In Jewish culture, the idea of God placing enemies under the feet of a king was a powerful image of victory and sovereignty. It also reflects the messianic expectations of the time, where the Messiah was to establish a reign of peace and justice.
35.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the certainty that all of Christ's enemies will ultimately be subjected to His authority. It reminds us that, although struggles exist in our Christian lives, the victory belongs to Christ, and He has the power to overcome all opposition.
35.commentaire: As believers, we must remember that our struggles are not in vain, for Christ has already won the victory. This verse encourages us to persevere in faith, knowing that even if we face spiritual enemies, God has a sovereign plan for our lives. We can live in the assurance that, ultimately, everything will be placed under the feet of our Lord.

mots.sens: The word 'Kyrios' means 'Lord' and is used to denote supreme authority. In the biblical context, it refers to the sovereignty of God and the lordship of Christ over all things. Acknowledging Jesus as 'Kyrios' emphasizes not only His divine power but also His role as Savior and King for humanity, which has profound implications for the Christian faith.

The term 'Christos' means 'Anointed' and is the equivalent of the Hebrew word 'Messiah'. It designates the one chosen and appointed by God to fulfill a salvific mission. In this verse, the affirmation that Jesus is the 'Christ' underscores His central role in God's plan of salvation, as the one sent to redeem humanity through His death and resurrection.

The word 'oikos' means 'house' and can refer to a family or a group of people living together. In the context of this verse, it refers to the community of Israel as a whole. The invitation to the entire house of Israel to recognize Jesus as Lord and Christ implies a collective responsibility to accept and respond to God's call for salvation.

The word 'stauros' means 'cross' and refers to the instrument of crucifixion used to execute Jesus. This term is laden with theological significance, as the cross represents both the suffering and sacrifice of Jesus for the sin of humanity. The mention of the crucifixion in this verse reminds us that redemption is obtained through the sacrifice of Christ, highlighting the importance of the cross in the Christian faith.

36.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, shortly after the resurrection of Jesus, in a context where the early Christians were preaching the Gospel in Jerusalem, facing a predominantly skeptical Jewish population.
36.passage: Acts 2 describes the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit descends upon the apostles, enabling them to speak in other languages. Peter, in his speech, proclaims the resurrection of Jesus and calls the listeners to recognize their guilt in His crucifixion.
36.culture: At that time, crucifixion was regarded as a shame and a curse, and the idea that one who had been crucified could be the Messiah was a scandal for many. The Jews were expecting a triumphant Messiah, which made Peter's message particularly provocative.
36.interpretation: The assertion that God made Jesus 'Lord and Christ' is a proclamation of His divine authority and salvific role. This calls each individual to a personal response to the truth of who Jesus is, recognizing both His divinity and His sacrifice.
36.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of recognizing Jesus not only as a teacher but as our Lord and Savior. As believers, we are called to live in response to this truth, witnessing to our faith and proclaiming the Gospel to those around us. Accepting Jesus as the Christ transforms our lives and commits us to follow His example of sacrifice and love.

mots.sens: This word means 'heart' and refers not only to the physical organ but also to the center of human emotions, thoughts, and will. In the spiritual context, it represents the depth of the human being, where true decisions and transformations occur. The fact that their hearts were 'touched' highlights a deep emotional and spiritual response to the truth proclaimed by Peter.

This verb means 'to have' or 'to possess', but in this context, it implies an awareness or possession of a feeling or conviction. The question 'What shall we do?' shows that they feel responsible and are seeking a concrete action to take in response to their awareness. This reveals a dynamic of personal transformation and active response to God's call.

This term means 'brothers' and indicates a relationship of brotherhood and belonging. In the context of the early Church, it emphasizes unity and solidarity among believers. By addressing Peter and the apostles as 'brothers', the listeners recognize a spiritual connection and a community of faith, essential for growth and mutual support in faith.

37.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, shortly after the resurrection of Jesus Christ, in a context where the early Christians were preaching the Gospel to the Jews of Jerusalem, marking the beginning of the Christian Church.
37.passage: In Acts 2, Peter preaches on the day of Pentecost, explaining the phenomenon of the Holy Spirit. This verse illustrates the reaction of the listeners to the announcement of the resurrection and their awareness of their need for repentance.
37.culture: At that time, Jewish culture valued repentance and returning to God, which makes the listeners' question very relevant. Their inquiry 'What shall we do?' reflects an expectation of a response to a call from God.
37.interpretation: The reaction of the listeners, touched in their hearts, shows the work of the Holy Spirit who convicts of sin and calls to repentance. Their question indicates a willingness to act and turn to God to receive forgiveness and new life.
37.commentaire: This verse teaches us the importance of responding to the word of God. When we are confronted with the truth of the Gospel, our hearts must be touched, prompting us to ask how we can respond to this call. This reminds us that the Christian faith is an active response to God's love and grace, urging us to act according to His will.

mots.sens: This term means a profound transformation of the mind and thought, often translated as 'repentance'. It implies a radical change of direction, an awareness of sins, and a sincere desire to turn away from them to turn towards God. In the context of this verse, repentance is essential for receiving forgiveness of sins, highlighting the importance of authentic conversion in the Christian life.

The word means 'baptism' and refers to the symbolic act of immersion in water, representing purification and identification with the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Baptism is a public declaration of faith and commitment to Christ, marking the beginning of a new life in Him. In this verse, it is linked to the forgiveness of sins, indicating that faith and obedience to the teaching of Jesus are essential for redemption.

This term means 'gift' and refers to a present or blessing offered unconditionally. In the context of this verse, it designates the Holy Spirit as a gift from God to those who repent and are baptized. This underscores divine generosity and the promise that the Holy Spirit will be present to guide and strengthen believers in their Christian walk.

38.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, shortly after the resurrection of Jesus, during the birth of the Christian Church in Jerusalem, in a context where the Jews were awaiting the Messiah and where the Holy Spirit was promised to believers.
38.passage: In Acts 2, Peter preaches on the day of Pentecost, explaining that the outpouring of the Holy Spirit is the fulfillment of prophecies. This verse is part of his call to repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, emphasizing the necessity of a personal response to the Gospel.
38.culture: At that time, baptism was a common practice in Jewish culture, symbolizing purification. However, baptism in the name of Jesus Christ introduces a new dimension, marking Christian identity and adherence to the community of believers.
38.interpretation: This verse teaches that repentance and baptism are essential steps to receive forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit. This underscores the importance of an active response to God's call to enter into a personal relationship with Him.
38.commentaire: This passage reminds us that repentance is not just regret, but a radical change of life. By turning to Christ and being baptized, we affirm our faith and our desire to live according to His will. By receiving the Holy Spirit, we are equipped to lead an authentic and dynamic Christian life, filled with His power.

mots.sens: This term means 'promise' and comes from the root 'ἀγγέλλω' (angello), which means 'to announce.' In the context of this verse, it refers to God's promise regarding the gift of the Holy Spirit. The theological significance of this word emphasizes God's faithfulness to His promises and the inclusivity of His call, not only for Peter's contemporaries but also for future generations.

This word means 'you' and directly addresses Peter's listeners. It underscores the idea that the promise of the Holy Spirit is not reserved for a select group but is for all who believe. This implies a personal and communal dimension of faith, where each individual is invited to receive God's gift.

This term means 'children' and evokes the idea of descent and continuity. In Jewish culture, children are often seen as heirs of God's promises. Spiritually, this emphasizes that the promise of the Holy Spirit extends not only to believers but also to their descendants, reinforcing the idea of passing on faith through generations.

This word means 'far' and indicates a geographical or temporal distance. In the context of this verse, it refers to all those who, throughout the ages and places, will be called by God. This highlights the universality of the gospel and the fact that God's call transcends cultural and geographical boundaries.

39.epoque: This verse was spoken shortly after the resurrection of Jesus, at a time when the early Christians were beginning to gather in Jerusalem, marking the beginning of the Christian Church.
39.passage: In Acts 2, Peter preaches on the day of Pentecost, explaining that the Holy Spirit is the promised gift from God. This chapter describes the birth of the Church and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the believers.
39.culture: At that time, Jewish culture was deeply rooted in the promises of God made to Abraham and his people. Peter's listeners understood well the importance of divine promises and their implications for future generations.
39.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the promise of the Holy Spirit is accessible to all, without distinction. It reveals God's heart, desiring that every person, regardless of their background, can enter into a relationship with Him and receive His Spirit.
39.commentaire: The promise of the Holy Spirit is an invitation to all, including our children and future generations. It reminds us of our responsibility to pass on the faith and encourage others to respond to God's call. As believers, we must live with the certainty that God continues to call souls, and we must be faithful witnesses to this promise.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to save' or 'to preserve.' In the biblical context, it evokes not only physical deliverance but also spiritual restoration and reconciliation with God. The root of this word emphasizes the idea of safety and protection, which is essential in the message of the Gospel. Spiritually, this implies that salvation is a divine action that removes us from perdition and places us in a living relationship with Christ.

This term refers to a 'generation' or 'lineage.' It can denote a group of people living at a given time, often with connotations of behavior or character. In this verse, it is used to describe a perverse generation, highlighting a degraded moral state. Theologically, this invites reflection on the impact of collective sin and the necessity to distinguish oneself from such behaviors through faith in Christ.

This verb means 'to exhort' or 'to urge.' It implies an urgent and passionate call to action, often with a dimension of comfort or encouragement. In the context of this verse, it underscores the intensity and sincerity of Peter's call to his listeners to turn away from corruption. Spiritually, this reminds us of the importance of responding seriously to God's call to repentance and faith.

40.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, shortly after the resurrection of Jesus, in a context where the nascent Christian community faced major persecutions and cultural challenges.
40.passage: Acts 2 recounts the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit descends upon the disciples. Peter, filled with the Spirit, preaches powerfully, calling the listeners to repentance and faith in Christ.
40.culture: At that time, Jewish culture was marked by messianic expectations and religious tensions. Peter's listeners were influenced by deep religious traditions but also by a perverse and immoral Roman society.
40.interpretation: Peter's exhortation to 'save yourselves' is an urgent call to repentance and separation from a generation that rejects God. It highlights the individual responsibility to respond to God's call for salvation, despite surrounding negative influences.
40.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of turning away from values and behaviors that oppose God's will. As believers, we are called to live distinctly, witnessing our faith in a world often at odds with divine principles. Peter's exhortation encourages us to take our salvation seriously and to share this message of redemption with those around us.

mots.sens: The word 'παρὰ' means 'beside' or 'outside of.' In the context of this verse, it evokes the idea of closeness to the word of God, emphasizing that those who accept the word do not merely listen but actively commit to living according to it. This underscores the importance of a personal and engaged response to the divine call.

The term 'βαπτίζω' means 'to immerse' or 'to plunge.' In the context of Christian baptism, it represents identification with the death and resurrection of Christ, symbolizing a new birth. Baptism is thus a public act of faith that marks a decisive turning point in a believer's life, signifying entry into the community of faith.

The word 'μαθητής' translates to 'disciple' and refers to a learner or student. In the New Testament, it refers to those who follow Jesus and commit to learning from His teachings. This implies an active and dynamic relationship with the Master, highlighting the importance of spiritual formation in the Christian life.

The word 'ψυχή' refers to the soul or life. In this verse, it indicates that the number of disciples increased by about three thousand souls, thus highlighting the spiritual and eternal dimension of each individual touched by the word of God. This reminds us that each conversion is precious and that every soul matters to God.

41.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the first Christian community, shortly after the resurrection of Jesus, in Jerusalem during the feast of Pentecost, a key moment in Christian history.
41.passage: Acts 2 recounts the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles and Peter's preaching, which leads to the massive conversion of the listeners. This verse highlights the immediate and powerful impact of the Gospel on those who hear and accept the word.
41.culture: At that time, baptism was a common practice in various religious traditions, but Christian baptism took on new significance, symbolizing purification and commitment to Christ. The Jewish community was already accustomed to purification rituals, which facilitated the acceptance of this new practice.
41.interpretation: This verse illustrates the power of the proclamation of the Gospel and the joyful response of those who accept the truth of God's word. The increase in the number of disciples shows that the Holy Spirit operates powerfully in hearts, transforming lives and adding souls to the Church.
41.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of sharing the Gospel and responding to God's call. By accepting the word and being baptized, believers commit to a new life in Christ, marked by community and witness. As Christians, we are called to live our faith authentically and to testify to the transformation that Christ works in us.

mots.sens: This term means 'teaching' and refers to the act of imparting knowledge, particularly that of the apostles. It involves formal instruction and spiritual training, emphasizing the importance of Christian doctrine in the life of the Church. In the context of this verse, it highlights the necessity of a solid foundation in faith for the community of believers.

This word translated as 'fellowship' evokes a deep and shared relationship among community members. It expresses the idea of mutual participation and sharing, both materially and spiritually. Theologically, it underscores the unity and solidarity that should exist among believers, reflecting the very nature of the Trinity.

This term means 'breaking' and refers to the act of breaking bread, often associated with the Lord's Supper. It symbolizes not only the physical sharing of bread but also the spiritual communion with Christ and among the members of the Church. In this verse, it reminds us of the importance of remembering Christ's sacrifice and the communion that flows from it.

This word means 'prayer' and denotes the act of addressing God. It involves personal and communal communication with the Lord, essential for spiritual life. In the context of this verse, it shows that prayer is a pillar of the life of the Church, connecting believers in their quest for God.

42.epoque: This passage is set at the beginning of the Christian Church, shortly after Pentecost, when the first disciples began to gather for worship and learning together.
42.passage: In Acts 2, Peter preaches the message of the Gospel, and about three thousand souls are added to the Church. Verse 42 describes the fundamental practices that unite these new believers.
42.culture: At this time, Jewish culture valued community and religious teaching. The believers, coming from Judaism, brought with them traditions of sharing and prayer, integrating these elements into their new faith in Christ.
42.interpretation: This verse illustrates the four pillars of Christian communal life: teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer. Together, they form a solid foundation for spiritual growth and the unity of believers.
42.commentaire: Acts 2:42 reminds us of the importance of persevering in our faith and spiritual practices. As a community, we must engage in the teaching of the Word, live in fellowship with one another, share the Lord's Supper, and pray together. This strengthens and unites us as the body of Christ, enabling us to fully live out our calling as disciples.

mots.sens: This word means 'fear' or 'awe', but it also carries a connotation of respect and wonder. In the biblical context, it evokes an attitude of reverence toward God, recognizing His power and holiness. The fear mentioned here is not a paralyzing fear, but a deep respect that incites worship and submission.

This term translates as 'wonder' or 'miracle', designating extraordinary events that provoke astonishment. Miracles are often associated with divine action and testify to God's presence among His people. In this verse, they serve to strengthen the faith of believers and draw the attention of non-believers to God's power.

The word 'sign' indicates an event or action that has a particular significance, often used to attest to the truth of a divine message. In the context of miracles, these signs are manifestations of God's authority and the truth of the Gospel. They serve to confirm the apostles' mission and establish the credibility of their testimony.

43.epoque: This passage is set at the beginning of the Christian Church, shortly after Pentecost, when the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, began their public ministry in Jerusalem.
43.passage: Acts 2 describes the birth of the Church and the events that follow Peter's preaching. Verse 43 highlights the spiritual impact and dynamics of the nascent Christian community, marked by the fear of God and miracles.
43.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, wonders and miracles were often associated with divine presence and the authority of prophets. The believers of this time expected signs that would confirm God's work among them.
43.interpretation: The fear that came upon everyone testifies to an awareness of God's power through the apostles. The miracles and wonders are not merely spectacular events, but signs of God's active presence in the lives of believers, strengthening their faith and unity.
43.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of living in the fear of God, an attitude that drives us to recognize His greatness and sovereignty. As Christians today, we must seek God's power in our lives and be open to His miracles, while cultivating a community founded on faith, respect, and wonder before His majesty.

mots.sens: The word 'koinonia' means 'sharing', 'fellowship', or 'association'. It evokes a deep and intimate relationship among believers, emphasizing the idea of unity and solidarity. In the context of the Christian community, this term highlights mutual responsibility and the commitment to live together according to the principles of the Gospel, thereby strengthening the body of Christ.

The term 'pisteuontes' derives from the verb 'pisteuō', meaning 'to believe' or 'to have faith'. In this verse, it designates those who have placed their trust in Jesus Christ. This word emphasizes not only the act of faith but also the transformation that occurs in the lives of believers, making them participants in a new community united by their common faith.

44.epoque: The passage is set at the beginning of the Christian Church, shortly after Pentecost, when the first disciples received the Holy Spirit and began to preach the Gospel. It is a time of rapid growth and spiritual enthusiasm.
44.passage: Acts 2:44 is found in a chapter that describes the birth of the Church and how the believers lived together, sharing their possessions and their faith. This verse illustrates the unity and solidarity that characterized this new community.
44.culture: In the Jewish and Greco-Roman context of the time, sharing possessions and communal living were important values. The early Christians radically reinterpreted these concepts in light of the Gospel, creating a model of communal life based on love and mutual support.
44.interpretation: This verse reveals the essence of Christian life: an authentic communion among believers, founded on their faith in Christ. It underscores the importance of living together, not only by sharing material resources but also by encouraging one another spiritually.
44.commentaire: The verse calls us to reflect on our own commitment to the faith community. Are we willing to share our resources and support our brothers and sisters in Christ? By living in unity and sharing, we testify to God's love and the power of the Gospel in our daily lives.

mots.sens: This term refers to properties or material goods. It comes from the root 'ktizō', which means 'to acquire' or 'to possess'. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the idea of detachment from material possessions for the benefit of the community, thus illustrating the importance of solidarity and sharing in Christian life. Theologically, this reflects Jesus' teaching on generosity and love for one's neighbor.

This word means 'need' or 'necessity'. It evokes a situation where help is required, often related to difficult circumstances. In this verse, it highlights the collective responsibility of believers to respond to the needs of others, thus underscoring the communal nature of the Church. Spiritually, it reminds us that Christian love is manifested through concrete actions towards those who are suffering.

This verb means 'to share' or 'to distribute'. It is derived from 'meris', which means 'part' or 'portion'. The use of this term in the verse indicates a voluntary act of sharing, where members of the Christian community take care of one another. It evokes a dynamic of giving and reciprocity, essential in the life of the Church.

45.epoque: This passage is set at the beginning of the Christian Church, shortly after Pentecost, when the first disciples began to gather and live together in community. It is a period marked by intense spiritual fervor and a deep commitment of believers to their faith and to one another.
45.passage: In Acts 2, the chapter describes the coming of the Holy Spirit and Peter's first sermon. This verse illustrates the believers' response to apostolic teaching, highlighting their commitment to live in community, sharing not only their faith but also their material resources.
45.culture: At that time, Jewish culture valued solidarity and mutual aid, especially in times of crisis. The early Christian communities took this value and integrated it into their practice, creating a new norm of sharing and mutual support that transcended social and economic divisions.
45.interpretation: This verse teaches us that the Christian life involves a commitment to respond to the needs of others. The sharing of material goods is not only an act of generosity but an expression of Christian love that reflects the character of Christ, who gave His life for us.
45.commentaire: The passage from Acts 2:45 reminds us of the importance of community in the Christian faith. By sharing our resources, we bear witness to God's love and our commitment to our brothers and sisters. It prompts us to reflect on our own attitude towards our possessions and to consider how we can serve those in need around us.

mots.sens: This term refers to communion or mutual participation among believers. It evokes a deep and intimate relationship, where each member of the community shares not only material goods but also spiritual experiences. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the importance of unity and solidarity within the early Church, manifested through acts of sharing and mutual support.

This word means 'joy' and refers to a state of inner happiness that transcends external circumstances. In biblical culture, joy is often linked to the presence of God and the recognition of His blessings. In this verse, it emphasizes that the joy of believers stems from their communion with Christ and their communal life, thereby strengthening their testimony to the world.

This term means 'simplicity' or 'sincerity' and evokes an attitude of heart without duplicity or hypocrisy. It suggests an authentic and selfless approach in relationships among believers. In the context of this verse, it reminds us that the Christian life should be lived with transparency and honesty that reflect the nature of Christ.

This word refers to the assembly or community of believers. It comes from the verb 'ekkaléo', which means 'to call out'. It underscores the fact that the Church is a gathering of those who have been called by God to live together as the body of Christ. In this verse, it highlights the importance of communal life and collective worship.

46.epoque: This verse is set in the context of the early Church, shortly after Pentecost, when the first Christians sought to establish their identity and common way of life as disciples of Jesus.
